title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
wiki_lead:
The Garden of Earthly Delights (Dutch: De tuin der lusten, lit. 'The garden of lusts') is the modern title given to a five-panel triptych (three oil-painted panels when open, two oak panels when closed) painted by the Early Netherlandish master Hieronymus Bosch, painted between 1490 and 1510, when Bosch was between 40 and 60 years old. Because of Bosch's religious beliefs, interpretations of the work typically assume it is a warning against the perils of temptation. The outer panels place the work on the Third Day of Creation. The intricacy of its symbolism, particularly that of the central panel, has led to a wide range of scholarly interpretations over the centuries.
Twentieth-century art historians are divided as to whether the triptych's central panel is a moral warning or a panorama of the paradise lost. He painted three large triptychs (the others are The Last Judgment of c. 1482 and The Haywain Triptych of c. 1516) that can be read from left to right and in which each panel was essential to the meaning of the whole. Each of these three works presents distinct yet linked themes addressing history and faith. Triptychs from this period were generally intended to be read sequentially, the left and right panels often portraying Eden and the Last Judgment respectively, while the main subject was contained in the centerpiece.
It is not known whether The Garden was intended as an altarpiece, but the general view is that the extreme subject matter of the inner center and right panels make it unlikely that it was planned for a church or monastery. It has been housed in the Museo del Prado in Madrid, Spain since 1939.

Description


Exterior

When the triptych's wings are closed, the design of the outer panels becomes visible. Rendered in a green–gray grisaille, these panels lack colour, probably because most Netherlandish triptychs were thus painted, but possibly indicating that the painting reflects a time before the creation of the sun and moon, which were formed, according to Christian theology, to "give light to the earth". The typical grisaille blandness of Netherlandish altarpieces served to highlight the splendid color inside.
The outer panels are generally thought to depict the creation of the world, showing greenery beginning to clothe the still-pristine Earth. God, wearing a crown similar to a papal tiara (a common convention in Netherlandish painting), is visible as a tiny figure at the upper left. Bosch shows God as the father sitting with a Bible on his lap, creating the Earth in a passive manner by divine fiat. Above him is inscribed a quote from Psalm 33:9 reading "Ipse dīxit, et facta sunt: ipse mandāvit, et creāta sunt"—For he spoke and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast. There is a firmament around the Earth, in reference to Genesis 1:7. It hangs suspended in the cosmos, which is shown as an impermeable darkness, whose only other inhabitant is God himself.
Despite the presence of vegetation, the earth does not yet contain human or animal life, indicating that the scene represents the events of the biblical Third Day. Bosch renders the plant life in an unusual fashion, using uniformly gray tints, which make it difficult to determine whether the subjects are purely vegetal or perhaps include some mineral formations. Surrounding the interior of the globe is the sea, partially illuminated by beams of light shining through clouds. The exterior wings have a clear position within the sequential narrative of the work as a whole. They show an unpopulated earth composed solely of rock and plants, contrasting sharply with the inner central panel, which contains an Earth teeming with lustful humanity.


Interior

Bosch may have intended the outer panels to establish a Biblical setting for the inner elements of the work, and the exterior image is generally interpreted as set in an earlier time than those in the interior. grok_lead: The Garden of Earthly Delights is a renowned oil-on-oak-panel triptych painted by the Early Netherlandish artist Hieronymus Bosch around 1490â1500, measuring 185.8 cm in height by 325.5 cm in width when fully open (central panel 172.5 cm wide, each wing 76.5 cm wide). Housed in the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid since 1933, the work unfolds across three interior panelsâdepicting the Creation in Eden, a surreal vision of human indulgence in a fantastical garden, and the torments of Hellâwhile its exterior wings feature a grisaille scene of the Third Day of Creation from Genesis. This masterpiece exemplifies Bosch's intricate, allegorical style, blending biblical themes with imaginative, often erotic and grotesque elements to explore morality and the human condition. Hieronymus Bosch, born Jheronimus van Aken around 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch, Netherlands, came from a family of painters and was active during the late 15th and early 16th centuries. The triptych likely originated in the southern Netherlands, possibly commissioned for a noble patron such as the court of the Duke of Burgundy, though its exact purpose remains debated among scholars. Its provenance traces back to the early 16th century, when it entered the collection of Engelbert II of Nassau; by 1591, it had been acquired by Philip II of Spain and housed at the monastery of El Escorial before its transfer to the Prado. First documented in detail in 1517 by the Italian diplomat Antonio de Beatis, the painting gained widespread fame posthumously, inspiring numerous copies and influencing later artists with its visionary imagery. The left panel portrays God presenting Eve to Adam in a verdant paradise teeming with exotic animals, symbolizing innocence and divine order before the Fall. The central panel, the work's most enigmatic section, shows multitudes of nude figuresâmen, women, and hybrid creatures âengaging in playful, sensual activities amid oversized fruits, fountains, and bizarre architectural forms, evoking a corrupted Eden where earthly pleasures blur into sin. In stark contrast, the right panel depicts a nightmarish Hell, filled with demonic tortures, musical instruments repurposed as instruments of punishment, and grotesque figures like the iconic "Tree Man," underscoring themes of damnation and moral retribution. Scholars interpret the triptych as a cautionary allegory warning against carnal temptation, drawing on medieval Christian theology while showcasing Bosch's unparalleled invention in Northern Renaissance art. Beyond its artistic innovation, The Garden of Earthly Delights has endured as a cultural icon, referenced in literature, music, and modern media for its surrealism and psychological depth. Conservation efforts at the Prado, including a major restoration in the 20th century, have preserved its vivid colors and fine details, allowing ongoing study of Bosch's techniques, such as his use of layered glazes and symbolic motifs. The painting's complexity continues to captivate, with exhibitions like the 2016 Bosch quincentenary at the Prado drawing record crowds and reaffirming its status as one of the most analyzed works in Western art history.
